newsitem.title: UK: Dollar licks wounds in Europe after Asian mauling.
newsitem.headline: Dollar licks wounds in Europe after Asian mauling.

text.p: The dollar licked its wounds in early Europe after fresh Japanese verbal intervention and escalating fears of a rate rise in Japan pummelled it overnight.
The U.S. currency was off Asian lows of 122.50 yen and 1.6977 marks as European traders took over the baton, but near-term omens looked grim for the dollar, analysts said.
"It's clear Japanese officials are continuing to try to talk down the dollar...there is scope for further falls against the yen," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International.
Japan's finance minister said overnight that intervention must be done jointly with other nations to be effective.
But the market's dollar-selling reaction to Japan's recent barrage of yen-positive comments means physical central bank action looks unnecessary, analysts said.
"The fact the dollar has weakened following concern by Japanese officials suggests there's no need for them to intervene," said Stamenkovic.
Traders said the dollar was unsettled by an article in Japanese financial daily Nikkei Kinyu speculating on chances of an official discount rate rise in July.
The story suggested some in the Bank of Japan may think the country's low interest rate policy should end soon.
"A new factor is now affecting sentiment, and that is talk of a Japanese rate hike this summer," said Klaus Baader, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"A stabilisation of the dollar would appear about the most bullish one would want to be for the short-term outlook."

Piling the pressure on the dollar was Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, who expressed hopes that markets would "further digest" the G7's accord in late April, which agreed to monitor exchange rates and cooperate as appropriate.
The dollar was quoted at 122.80/90 yen at 0807 GMT, down from late Thursday's European level of 123.70/80.
Dollar/mark was rattled by dollar/yen's weakness, but the feeling that Germany is less concerned than Japan about current forex levels limited the damage, analysts said.
It was also supported by a slide in mark/yen to a nearly two-month low of 71.98 from 72.47/50. The dollar stood at 1.7037/47 marks at 0825 GMT versus late yesterday's 1.7071/76.
The growing speculation of a Japanese rate rise is an added burden on dollar/yen as players fret over whether or not the U.S. Federal Reserve will tighten after its May 20 meeting.
Fed chairman Alan Greenspan gave food for thought when he spoke overnight -- but market reaction was confused.
Greenspan said he expected economic growth to slow later this year and into next, but the Fed would need to act if that did not turn out to be the case.
Greenspan, who called the Fed's quarter-point rate rise after its last meeting in March "a form of insurance", said there was scant evidence of an imminent resurgence of inflation.
But labour markets were growing tighter and the economy had little slack, he warned.
Some market watchers felt the comments weakened the chances of a May 20 rate rise, while others said Greenspan had said nothing to suggest policy would not be tightened pre-emptively.

"The even-handed comments leave the question of a May 20 rate hike open. On balance, we would expect to see a further 25 basis-point tightening," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist for Europe at BankAmerica in London.
With no U.S. data due out today, the market must wait until next week for new clues on which way the Fed will swing.

U.S. April retail sales are due on Tuesday, with producer prices on Wednesday. April CPI, capacity utilisation, industrial production and real earnings appear on Thursday, with housing starts and the Philadelphia Fed survey following on Friday.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
